title: Feed your soil, save water and manage pests safely
course_title: Sustainable Agriculture Practices: Healthy Soil, Smart Water and Climate-Ready Farming

say: Feed your soil, save water, and manage pests safely.
This is the video for Module 2 of Sustainable Agriculture Practices.
Compost needs greens, which are fresh, like peels and manure, and browns, which are dry, like stalks and dry leaves. Use about two to three parts browns to one part greens.
Step one. Choose a shaded spot near water.

panel.heading: Building a compost heap
items: Shaded spot; pit in dry areas, heap in wet
Base of coarse sticks, about 15 cm
Layers: browns, greens and manure, old soil
Moist like a squeezed-out sponge
About 1 m wide and 1 m high, covered
Turn every one to two weeks

say: Step two. Lay coarse sticks about 15 cm deep, so air enters from below.

panel.heading: Building a compost heap

say: Step three. Add browns, then greens and manure, then a sprinkle of old soil to bring in soil organisms.

panel.heading: Building a compost heap

say: Step four. Water each layer until moist, not dripping.

panel.heading: Building a compost heap
items: Shaded spot; pit in dry areas, heap in wet
Base of coarse sticks, about 15 cm

say: Step five. Build it about 1 m wide and 1 m high, and cover it against sun and heavy rain.

panel.heading: Building a compost heap
items: Shaded spot; pit in dry areas, heap in wet
Base of coarse sticks, about 15 cm
Layers: browns, greens and manure, old soil

say: Step six. After a week, push a stick into the centre. Warm means it is working. Turn it every one to two weeks. It is ready in about two to three months.
Manure can carry germs, so wear gloves or wash well with soap.

panel.rule: Never use human, dog or cat faeces. Wash hands after manure.

say: Mulch is a blanket of dry grass, stalks or leaves. It stops crusting, slows evaporation and smothers weeds. Spread it 5 to 10 cm thick, away from stems.

panel.heading: Mulch, legumes and rotation
items: Mulch 5 to 10 cm thick, off the stems
Legumes fix nitrogen: pink nodules
Rotate crop families every season
Never tomato after pepper or garden egg

say: Legumes such as cowpea, groundnut and soybean fix nitrogen. Cut a nodule open at flowering. Pink or red inside means it is working.

panel.heading: Mulch, legumes and rotation
items: Mulch 5 to 10 cm thick, off the stems
Legumes fix nitrogen: pink nodules
Rotate crop families every season
Never tomato after pepper or garden egg

say: Rotate: cereal, then legume, then fruit vegetable, then a leaf or root crop.

panel.heading: Mulch, legumes and rotation
items: Mulch 5 to 10 cm thick, off the stems
Legumes fix nitrogen: pink nodules
Rotate crop families every season
Never tomato after pepper or garden egg

say: And never follow tomato with pepper, garden egg or Irish potato. They are one family and share diseases like bacterial wilt.

say: Catch rain where it falls. Planting pits, about 20 to 40 cm across with compost in each, collect runoff around the roots.

panel.heading: Catch rain where it falls
items: Planting pits with compost in each
Half-moons, open side facing uphill
Tied ridges: small basins hold rain
Rows and ridges across the slope
Roof water: 1 mm on 1 m² = 1 litre

say: Half-moons trap water running down a gentle slope.

say: From a metal roof, multiply the area by the rain in millimetres, then by 0.8. For example, Grace in Jos has a 48 square metre roof. One 25 mm rain gives about 960 litres, nearly filling her 1,000-litre tank.

say: Grace's 100 square metre tomato plot needs about 400 litres a day at its peak. With a watering can, only about 60 percent reaches the roots, so she must carry about 667 litres.

panel.heading: Grace's tomatoes: watering can or drip?

say: Drip delivers about 90 percent, so 444 litres is enough. Over 60 days that saves about 13,320 litres.
Before watering, squeeze a handful of soil from the root zone. Water only if it crumbles dry.

panel.heading: Grace's tomatoes: watering can or drip?

say: Cover every tank and drum with a lid or mesh so mosquitoes cannot breed. Fence open ponds and deep pits and never leave children alone near them. And never use untreated sewage or drainage water on vegetables eaten raw.

panel.heading: Water, mosquitoes and children
items: Cover every tank, drum and pot
Fence or cover ponds and deep pits
Never leave children alone near water
No sewage water on raw-eaten vegetables

say: Integrated pest management means prevent, watch, decide, then act with the least harmful option. Prevention comes first.

panel.heading: Scout before you spray
items: Prevent: rotation, clean seed, spacing
Walk a W pattern, five stops, 20 plants
Work out the percentage damaged
Below the action level: act by hand
Above it: targeted option, last resort

say: Once or twice a week, walk the field in a W pattern. At five stops, check 20 plants. For fall armyworm on maize, look for windowpane patches and sawdust-like droppings in the whorl.

panel.heading: Scout before you spray
items: Prevent: rotation, clean seed, spacing
Walk a W pattern, five stops, 20 plants
Work out the percentage damaged
Below the action level: act by hand
Above it: targeted option, last resort

say: For example, Bisi in Oyo State found 12 damaged plants out of 100. That is 12 percent.

panel.heading: Scout before you spray
items: Prevent: rotation, clean seed, spacing
Walk a W pattern, five stops, 20 plants
Work out the percentage damaged
Below the action level: act by hand
Above it: targeted option, last resort

say: Her officer's action level was 20 percent, so she crushed eggs and young larvae by hand and scouted again.

panel.heading: Scout before you spray
items: Prevent: rotation, clean seed, spacing
Walk a W pattern, five stops, 20 plants
Work out the percentage damaged
Below the action level: act by hand
Above it: targeted option, last resort

say: The next week it was 27 percent. She used one targeted option, registered for maize, only into the affected whorls. By week 5, damage fell to 8 percent. One treatment, not weekly spraying.

say: Buy only from a registered agro-dealer, with a NAFDAC number on the label. Read the label, including the days to wait before harvest. Wear full protection and never spray into the wind.
Pregnant or breastfeeding women and children should not mix or spray. Store pesticides locked away, and if someone feels ill, go to a health facility with the label.

panel.heading: Pesticide safety rules
items: Registered dealer, sealed, NAFDAC number
Read the label; never exceed the rate
Gloves, long sleeves, boots, eye cover
Calm weather, never into the wind
No mixing or spraying if pregnant
Locked away; never in drink bottles

say: To remember. Build compost with browns and greens. Mulch, and bring a legume into every cycle. Catch rain where it falls. Use drip to stretch water. And scout first, with chemicals last.

panel.heading: Remember
items: Compost: browns, greens, air, water, turning
Mulch thick; include a legume every cycle
Catch rain with pits, ridges and roofs
Drip stretches water much further
Scout first; chemicals last and safely

say: Now start a compost heap and plan four seasons of rotation. Make your water plan with a roof calculation. Then run a scouting week and work out your percentages.
